# Overview

replaylab decides **which designed proteins to send to a wet lab**. A game
gives a player (a scripted policy or a language-model agent) a pool of designs
with predicted metrics and a budget. Each round the player buys a batch, the lab
reports which designs bind, and the player decides what to buy next or whether
to stop. Offline, the lab is a **replay** of recorded outcomes from Adaptyv's
Proteinbase data; the same code is meant to drive a live campaign later.

This page follows the data from the raw CSV to a scored campaign, then shows how
the packages are layered and how the hidden outcomes are kept out of reach.

# From raw data to a game

The build scripts turn the Proteinbase export into three tables, derive the
sequence clusters and folds from them, and expose two things to a game: the pool
of designs with their visible features, and the hidden outcomes.

```{d2}
direction: right

csv: "proteinbase.csv"

tables: {
  label: "build_tables"
  designs: "designs (parquet)"
  outcomes: "outcomes (parquet)"
  targets: "targets (parquet)"
}

derived: {
  label: "derived tables"
  clusters: "clusters.csv"
  folds: "folds.csv"
}

pool: "DesignPool\n(visible features)"
hidden: "hidden outcomes"

csv -> tables
tables -> derived
tables -> pool
tables -> hidden
```

`data/build_clusters.py` and `data/build_folds.py` write the two derived tables
under `data/splits/`, where they are committed and treated as frozen: `--check`
only compares against the committed summary and prints `OK` or `DIFF`, and
overwriting either file takes `--force`.

**Clusters group variants of the same design.** Each sequence becomes a binary
3-mer vector (`kmer_matrix`), designs within cosine distance 0.4 of each other
are linked, and a cluster is a connected component of those links. Designs that
close are almost always one family, often by one author. Clusters serve two
offline purposes:

* **Cutting the split.** A family is never divided across folds, so no design
  sits in the held-out set while its close relatives sit in a development game.
* **Scoring.** `ScoreCard.distinct_families` counts how many clusters the hits
  came from: four hits in one family is a different result from four hits in
  four families.

Clusters never inform a decision. They live on `DesignPool` and in the scoring
context, not on `CampaignState`, and no tool returns one. An agent gets
`similar_designs` instead: the same 3-mer geometry, computed live over the
campaign's designs and returned only as similarity values.

**Folds are the train/test split.** Each design of a target is assigned to one of
three folds with `StratifiedGroupKFold`, using its cluster as the *group* (a
family stays whole) and its hit label as the *label* (hit rates stay equal). The
builder tries seeds until all three folds are within ±2 designs and ±2 hits of
each other. **Fold 2 is held out.** This gives the three splits used in
`config/games.yaml`: `dev` (folds 0 and 1), `heldout` (fold 2) and `all`, which
ignores folds (the stop games, `E` and `E-long`).

Because the split is committed rather than drawn at run time, `folds.csv` is an
argument to `build_replay_campaign`: it decides **which designs a game
contains**, and both `load_pool` and `load_outcomes` filter through it. No model
is cross-validated on the folds; a model is only ever fitted on what a campaign
has bought.

**What `data/splits/` holds.** Three committed files, all keyed by Proteinbase's
public design ids (names such as `amber-crow-willow`), with no sequences and no
outcomes:

* `clusters.csv`: the cluster of every design;
* `folds.csv`: the fold of every design;
* `nipah_heldout_ids.txt`: the 343 Nipah-G design ids of fold 2, one per line.
  `data/build_folds.py` writes it next to `folds.csv`, and a data test checks
  that it matches fold 2 exactly. No code reads it at run time; it is there so
  the held-out set can be inspected and audited without loading the tables.

Committing real ids does not break the leak rules: those rules govern what a
*player* sees, and players only ever see per-seed aliases. Anyone with the public
Proteinbase data could rebuild these files anyway; committing them freezes the
split so every run uses the same one.

# Playing a campaign

`build_replay_campaign` assembles a game for one seed: it loads the pool and the
hidden outcomes for the game's split and assigns the per-seed aliases. Each
round, the player reads a `CampaignState` snapshot and chooses a batch;
`Campaign.submit` records it and advances the clock, and the replay backend
delivers the outcomes that are due. After the last round, `settle` collects any
outcomes still pending and `score` produces a `ScoreCard`.
[How a game is played](03-playing.qmd) follows this loop and the life of one
batch in detail.

```{d2}
direction: down

setup: "build_replay_campaign\n(game + seed)"

round: "each round" {
  grid-columns: 2
  grid-gap: 70
  state: "CampaignState\nsnapshot"
  choose: "policy or agent\nchooses a batch"
  poll: "ReplayBackend.poll\ndue outcomes arrive"
  submit: "Campaign.submit\nclock ticks"
  state -> choose
  choose -> submit
  submit -> poll
  poll -> state
}

score: "settle + score\n→ ScoreCard"

setup -> round
round -> score: "after the\nlast round"
```

# Package layers

The packages fall into two groups: the *world* that defines and plays a game,
and the *players* and *drivers* that act on it. In the two charts below, an
arrow means **may import**, not data flow: `a → b` means package `a` is allowed
to import package `b`. The map is enforced by `tests/test_import_boundaries.py`,
which fails the build when a package imports outside its lane.

**The world.** `engine` holds the game rules and wires everything else together.
Every package ends at `domain`, which imports nothing from replaylab (standard
library only) and holds the shared vocabulary: `Design`, `Outcome`,
`CampaignState` and the feature specs. It is the floor the other packages stand
on, not a funnel things flow into.

```{d2}
vars: {
  d2-config: {
    layout-engine: elk
  }
}

direction: down
engine: "engine\ngame rules"
store: "store\nSQLite"
backends: "backends\ndeliver outcomes"
datasets: "datasets\npools, similarity"
config: "config\nYAML loading"
domain: "domain\ncore types · stdlib only"
engine -> store
engine -> backends
engine -> datasets
engine -> config
datasets -> config
store -> domain
backends -> domain
datasets -> domain
config -> domain
```

**Players and drivers.** `interfaces` exposes the 15 tools over MCP and the
command line; it may import every package, and none may import it back.
`eval` runs experiments and may import anything (dashed). The agent side,
`policies` and `advisor`, may import neither `engine`, `store` nor `backends`.
`domain` is omitted here for clarity: every package may import it.

```{d2}
direction: down
interfaces: "interfaces\n15 tools · MCP server · CLI"
eval: "eval\nruns experiments"
policies: "policies"
advisor: "advisor"
world: "engine · store · backends"
datasets: "datasets"

interfaces -> policies
interfaces -> world
eval -> policies: {style.stroke-dash: 4}
eval -> world: {style.stroke-dash: 4}
policies -> advisor
advisor -> datasets
world -> datasets
policies -> world: "may not import" {
  style.stroke: "#c0392b"
  style.font-color: "#c0392b"
  style.stroke-dash: 3
}
```

::: {.callout-note}
**The rule that matters:** `advisor` and `policies` never import `store`,
`backends` or `engine`. They receive a
[`CampaignState`](../reference/domain.CampaignState.qmd) snapshot and nothing
else, so they *cannot* write to the campaign and *cannot* see an outcome it has
not bought. This is the architectural half of the leak protection; the rest is
described below.
:::

# The leak rules

A hidden outcome must never reach a player before it buys the design. Three
independent layers enforce this:

1. **Architecture.** The import boundaries above: players see snapshots only.
2. **API shape.** The [`ReplayBackend`](../reference/backends.ReplayBackend.qmd)
   releases an outcome only through `Campaign.submit` followed by
   `ReplayBackend.poll`, once its delay has passed. There is no bulk accessor to
   leak through.
3. **Guards.** `load_outcomes` refuses to read the held-out split outside the
   final run (`HeldOutAccessError`). A held-out game must be a final-test game,
   so the evaluation runner plays it only with `--final-run`, once, under a lock,
   and every other entry point refuses it. Real design ids never appear in the
   state or in any file the store writes: players see `d0001`-style aliases.

These layers hold against code that uses the public API. Inside one Python
process nothing is truly private: the campaign holds the backend, and the
backend holds every outcome. Why that is still a real boundary for the LLM agent,
and only a checked convention for scripted policies, is explained in
[What keeps the results hidden](03-playing.qmd#what-keeps-the-results-hidden).

# Persistence and kill-and-resume

The [`CampaignStore`](../reference/store.CampaignStore.qmd) (SQLite) writes
every change in a single transaction, and batches only move forward:
`proposed → submitted → partial → complete`. Alongside the tables it keeps an
**append-only event log**. `build_replay_campaign` replays that log to rebuild
the replay backend's exact state, so a process killed mid-campaign resumes where
it stopped and ends in *exactly* the same state as an uninterrupted run (tested
with delays of 0 and 2 rounds).

# Determinism

replaylab uses no global random state, never calls `hash()` on strings, and
never lets dict or set ordering reach its output. All randomness comes from a
seeded `numpy.random.Generator` passed in explicitly (`make_rng(seed, round)`),
so the same state and seed always produce the same batch. This is what makes the
100-seed evaluation tables reproducible.
